study_identification_part.si4_title: Accommodating Site Variation In Neuroimaging Data Using Normative And Hierarchical Bayesian Models

cm1_research_objectives.reason: The study clearly states its research objectives and the purpose of applying normative modeling. The study aims to develop a method for applying normative modeling to neuroimaging datasets affected by site effects resulting from pooling data between sites. The purpose is explicitly described: to create reliable normative models in multi-site neuroimaging data by including site as a predictor in a hierarchical Bayesian framework, rather than using two-step harmonization approaches. The abstract states the aim is to accommodate site effects by including them as random effects in a hierarchical Bayesian model, and the introduction clearly describes the objective of developing normative models that can handle site variation while retaining clinically useful information. Both criteria are satisfied: (1) research hypotheses/questions are provided - testing whether hierarchical Bayesian models outperform harmonization techniques for dealing with site effects; (2) the purpose of applying normative modeling is described - to enable individualized predictions while accounting for site effects in multi-site data.
cm1_research_objectives.supporting_text: In this study, we suggest accommodating for these site effects by including them as random effects in a hierarchical Bayesian model. | In this work, we aimed to provide a method that allows the application of normative modeling to neuroimaging data sets that are affected by site effects resulting from pooling data between sites. | The potential of normative modeling to make individualized predictions from neuroimaging data has enabled inferences that go beyond the case-control approach.
cm1_research_objectives.location: Abstract and Discussion section, main paper

nm1_selection_criteria_reference_cohort.reason: This study builds a NEW normative model using the ABIDE dataset. All three criteria for NEW normative models are satisfied: (1) Eligibility criteria are described - the study uses 569 healthy controls from the ABIDE consortium, which is a publicly available dataset. The original ABIDE data collection and preprocessing procedures are referenced (Di Martino et al., 2014; Craddock et al., 2013). (2) Image quality standards are specified - the study describes outlier detection procedures: 'The criterion applied to mark a value as an outlier was if it was above or beyond 2 inter quartile ranges from the mean of all values for that region and hemisphere.' This procedure removed 1055 out of 162905 data points (0.006%). (3) Final sample size and reasons for exclusion are reported - the study states it used 569 controls for model development (out of 573 available), with 470 males. The supplement explains that sample sizes differed between models due to missing value requirements: ComBat Gam required complete data, reducing the sample from 391 to 370 in training and 168 to 156 in test set. The normative modeling process handled missing values region-wise.
nm1_selection_criteria_reference_cohort.supporting_text: The ABIDE consortium (http://preprocessed-connectomes-project.org/abide/) was founded to facilitate research and collaboration on autism spectrum disorders by data aggregation and sharing. The consortium provides a publicly available structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data set and corresponding phenotypic information of 539 individuals with autism spectrum disorder and 573 age-matched typical controls. For this study, we used 569 controls for development and performance testing of the models, out of which 470 were male. | The criterion applied to mark a value as an outlier was if it was above or beyond 2 inter quartile ranges from the mean of all values for that region and hemisphere. This quite liberal criterion was applied with the aim to detect not outliers in a mathematical sense (+/- 95 % confidence interval), but to detect impossible values. This leads to the removal of 1055 out of 162905 data points (0.006%) of all values. | Despite the aim of the study to run all seven models in this study on the same data set, we were faced with the challenge that differing requirements for each model with respect to missing values made an adjustment of sample sizes per model necessary.
nm1_selection_criteria_reference_cohort.location: Section 3.1.1 (ABIDE data set), Section 3.2 (Pre-processing), and Supplementary Material Section 0.1

nm2_handling_of_covariates_reference_coh.reason: Both criteria are satisfied for handling covariates in the reference cohort. (1) Covariates such as age and sex are explicitly considered in the normative models. The study states that age and sex are included as predictors in both the hierarchical Bayesian linear model (HBLM) and hierarchical Bayesian Gaussian process model (HBGPM). The models predict cortical thickness based on age, sex, and site. (2) Since multi-site data are used (20 sites from the ABIDE dataset), methods for addressing site effects are extensively described. The core methodological contribution of this paper is modeling site as a random effect in a hierarchical Bayesian framework. The study states: 'we include site as a random effect in the model' and 'site is modeled hierarchically, resulting in a random effect for site.' The hierarchical structure uses partial pooling where site-specific parameters share a common prior distribution. The paper compares this approach to other site harmonization methods (ComBat, regressing out site effects).
nm2_handling_of_covariates_reference_coh.supporting_text: we suggest accommodating for these site effects by including them as random effects in a hierarchical Bayesian model | In a hierarchical linear version of the model, site is modeled hierarchically, resulting in a random effect for site ('Hierarchical Bayesian Linear Model, HBLM'). | For modeling site effects, introducing a hierarchical structure has the benefit that it allows to include structural dependencies between sites via partial pooling.
